description.text: Aegon’s portfolio includes fully owned businesses in the Americas and the United Kingdom, a global asset manager, and a life insurer that serves affluent and high-net-worth individuals predominantly in Asia. Aegon also has insurance joint ventures in Spain & Portugal, China, and Brazil, and asset management partnerships in France and China, as well as a strategic shareholding in the Dutch insurance company a.s.r. Aegon allocates capital toward profitable opportunities across these markets and leverages the talent, knowledge, processes, and technologies of its different businesses. Aegon derives its revenue and earnings from insurance premiums, investment returns, fees, and commissions. Aegon is growing its direct and affiliated distribution capabilities to engage directly with customers.

about.description_short: Aegon is an international financial services holding company. Aegon's ambition is to become a leading US life insurance, annuity, and retirement group with international insurance and asset management subsidiaries. Aegon's portfolio of businesses includes fully-owned businesses in the United States and a global asset manager. On April 15, 2026, Aegon announced an agreement to sell its insurance platform in the UK, Aegon UK, and expects to complete the transaction around the end of 2026. Via insurance joint-ventures in Spain & Portugal, China, and Brazil, and via asset management partnerships in France and China, Aegon creates value by combining Aegon's international expertise with strong local partners. In addition, Aegon owns a Bermuda-based life insurer and generates value via a strategic shareholding in a market leading Dutch insurance and pensions company. Aegon's purpose of helping people live their best lives runs through all its activities.

analysis_md:
# AEG — AEGON LTD.
Engine 5.4 pass-1 run, 2026-10-17. Price $8.32 (nasdaq_quote_api); market cap est. $12,920,960,000 — in scope under $40B. EUR-reporting 20-F filer (CIK 769218); all engine figures are USD after period-end ECB conversion (see FX flag).

All figures below are copied from dcf_numbers.json, financials_history.csv, ttm.py output or fundamentals.json — none are recomputed.

## What it is
Bermuda-domiciled, Netherlands-headquartered life insurer in mid-transition to a US-centric group: Transamerica life/retirement in the Americas (including World Financial Group distribution), a UK platform, International strategic partnerships, and asset management. Shareholders approved redomiciliation to Delaware, a future Transamerica Inc. name, and a single share class in October 2026; the Dutch business was sold to a.s.r. in July 2023 and a UK sale has been agreed in company reporting. FY2025 company prints: net result EUR 980 million, operating result up 15%, dividend EUR 0.40/share for FY2025.

## Owner's earnings
**FY2025 (20-F via EDGAR, from financials_history.csv, after the two filing overrides below):** operating cash flow $509,950,000; capex $48,175,000; SBC $69,325,000 (override, EUR 59M at the 1.175 period-end rate).

## Moat: 4/10 — weak-to-narrow
Justification: Transamerica scale in US life and retirement, World Financial Group distribution passing 100,000 agents in H1 2026, and diversified Americas/UK/International/asset-management earnings — against commodity products, a shrinking perimeter, and returns that have not held above the cost of capital through a cycle.
- FOR: Transamerica scale in US life insurance and retirement, with World Financial Group distribution passing 100,000 agents in H1 2026; diversified earnings across Americas, UK, International strategic partnerships and asset management; operating momentum (FY2025 operating result up 15%, H1 2026 operating capital generation up 27% in company reporting); capital-return capacity (growing dividend, repeated buybacks, 169% group solvency at H1 2026); simplification path (US redomiciliation and Transamerica renaming approved October 2026, UK sale agreed).
- AGAINST: commodity life/retirement products sold on price and service — no demonstrated structural pricing power; returns below a clear moat standard (fundamentals.json ROE: FY2023 negative at −2.08% on its series, FY2024 7.26%, FY2025 10.32%); legacy blocks and market/IFRS finance swings drive net result and operating cash flow (OE/share range >3x over five years); shrinking perimeter (Dutch business sold 2023, UK sale pending — the scored revenue base contracts by design); capital-intensive, rate-sensitive, multi-jurisdiction regulation, plus redomiciliation/US-GAAP execution risk.
- ROIC evidence, as required: fundamentals.json's `roic_proxy` is null for FY2023–2025 and gross margin is not presented for an insurer (no COGS line), so neither series can support a moat of 7+; the ROE series above is the usable return history and it sits at/below a plausible cost of capital in two of the last three years. A 4 gives CAP = 7.2 years: growth holds 2 years, then converges linearly to the 2.5% terminal rate over 7.2 years, 15-year projection.

## Flags — every fragility flag resolved
- **DATA_GAP:sbc / DATA_GAP:shares / ADS_RATIO_MISSING**: resolved by the three filing overrides above; measured impact quoted there.
- **STALE_FY** (FY ended 9.5 months ago): ttm.py cannot compute a TTM for this IFRS filer (reported above), and Aegon reports semi-annually, so the median FY base is used per the worker spec for IFRS names. H1 2026 company reporting (operating result EUR 804M, up 9%; net result EUR 608M; operating capital generation EUR 416M, up 27%; free cash flow EUR 392M) shows operating improvement but no OE-yield inflection that changes the verdict at $8.32.
- **BASE_DIVERGENCE** (latest FY $0.2527 vs median $0.4362): the latest year is the depressed one — FY2025 operating cash flow fell to $509,950,000 even as net income rose, because the IFRS net result carried non-operating/investment effects (below). The median is the steadier base and is used; the divergence does not drive the verdict — even the median base yields only a 5.24% OE yield at $8.32, and on the latest-FY base the tier would be lower still.
- **NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE** (2023, 2025): FY2023 net income −$219,895,000 vs OCF +$954,720,000; FY2025 net income +$1,151,500,000 vs OCF +$509,950,000 (financials_history.csv). For an IFRS insurer the net result absorbs insurance-finance and investment fair-value moves and disposal effects that do not pass through operating cash flow in the same period — the filing's notes attribute FY2025 other income mainly to selling part of the a.s.r. stake (an investing inflow), and FY2023 was the a.s.r. transaction year itself. The OCF-based conservative OE is the series used throughout, so the divergence does not contaminate the base; it is why the base is OCF-based at all.
- **OE_VOLATILE** (OE/share range >3x over 5 years): real — FY2021 OE/share was negative on the filed history and FY2022 printed $1.7452 on the override share count. Handled with the normalized (median) base and the bear-shifted probabilities (45% bear-or-worse).
- **FX_CONVERTED**: EUR reporting converted at period-end ECB reference rates (FY2025 1.175, FY2024 1.0389, FY2023 1.105 — full table in dcf_numbers.json fx_conversion); flow facts use period-end, not period-average, rates. Noted as a basis limitation.
- **ADS_RATIO_APPLIED (x1.0)**: see OVERRIDES — NYRS are the common shares themselves, 1-for-1; no scaling applied.
- **SHARES_FALLBACK** (2016–2022): pre-2023 history years use the fallback counts recorded in financials_history.csv's shares_tag column; per-share history there is approximate and is not used for the gated base years.
- **BUYBACK_TAILWIND (preliminary run only)**: the preliminary run credited an 8.2%/yr share-count decline; after the shares override the history is flat by construction (single FY2025 count applied to all missing years), so the final blend carries no buyback credit. The buybacks are real in the filing (issued common shares fell from 1,814,727 thousand at end-2023 to 1,573,120 thousand at end-2025 in the share-capital note, with further buybacks through 2026 in company reporting) — the final run is therefore, if anything, conservative on this leg, and the gap to the hurdle is far wider than any buyback credit could close.
- **SECTOR_MODEL_MISMATCH**: confidence is **low**, as required. No tier_override is applied: the standing insurer-float softening applies when an OCF-based base capitalizes float and inflates the tier — here the base is not float-inflated (FY2025 OCF is below net income) and tier-by-numbers is already D, so there is nothing to soften. See method range below for the model's opposite blind spot.

## My thoughts / method range
- The honest headline is a range with a robust bottom line. On the engine's OCF-based owner's earnings this is a D by a wide margin: a 5.24% OE yield at $8.32 against a 15% hurdle, a super-bull case that still only returns 10.59%, and a hurdle price of $2.71.
- The known model blind spot cuts the other way and must be stated: insurers' distributable cash generation is better captured by operating capital generation (EUR 1.3 billion for FY2025 in company reporting) than by IFRS operating cash flow ($509,950,000), because insurance investment and contract flows route through the cash-flow statement differently. On an insurer-native capital-generation definition the shares would screen materially cheaper than $2.71 of IV. That is a reason to distrust the precise IV, not a reason to upgrade the tier inside this sweep's stated method — every insurer in the sweep is graded on the same OCF basis, and even a generous growth recalibration (bull/super-bull starts above) does not lift any scenario to 15%.
- What the market is actually pricing at $8.32 is the simplification story: US redomiciliation, Transamerica focus, UK exit, holding-cash release funding buybacks (H2 2026 buyback raised to EUR 350M in company reporting, funded partly from holding cash above target — a one-time resource, not a recurring OE stream), and a ~5%-plus dividend yield on the EUR 0.40 FY2025 dividend. None of that is owner's-earnings growth the DCF can underwrite at this price.
